title: Haemophilia
everyday_terms: bleeds a lot after a cut
summary: Haemophilia means the blood does not clot properly because a clotting protein is missing or low. Bleeding lasts longer, and in more severe forms bleeding can happen inside joints and muscles.
inheritance_plain: It is X-linked: the F8 gene (haemophilia A) or the F9 gene (haemophilia B) is on the X chromosome. Boys have one X, so one changed copy affects them. Girls have two X chromosomes and are usually carriers, though some have signs too. X-linked chances depend on which parent has the change, so a genetic counsellor talks them through with you.
carrier_meaning: A woman with one changed copy is called a carrier. Many carriers have no symptoms; some have milder effects, and a doctor can check for them.
disease_meaning: Haemophilia mostly affects boys and men. Modern treatment from specialist haemophilia centres prevents and treats bleeds, and many people live full, active lives.
screening: A genetic test can look for a change in the F8 gene (haemophilia A) or the F9 gene (haemophilia B). A genetic counsellor can explain who in a family might choose to be tested.
suggested_questions: Why is haemophilia more common in boys?
My brother has haemophilia. What could that mean for me?
What does a test for haemophilia involve?
card_summary: The blood doesn't clot properly, so bleeding lasts longer. Mostly affects males.
carrier_short: A changed copy on one X chromosome. Often no symptoms. Can pass it on.
disease_short: Blood doesn't clot properly. Treated at specialist haemophilia centres.
care: Specialist haemophilia centres, physiotherapy, genetic counselling and family support groups.
